artifacts.synopsis: The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session's reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2's sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession.

artifacts.title: Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

artifacts.synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

artifacts.synopsis: Three Teaching Elders complained against Pacific Presbytery's handling of TE Wilbourne's BCO 38-1 confession and subsequent deposition. The SJC sustained the complaints by reference to its decision in Case 2020-07.

artifacts.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

artifacts.synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

artifacts.synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

artifacts.title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

artifacts.title: Dale Cutler v. Platte Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC found that Presbytery of Siouxlands erred in denying a complaint that sought the appointment of a committee to conduct a BCO 31-2 investigation into whether TE Greg Lawrence held or taught views associated with Federal Vision theology contrary to the PCA's doctrinal standards. The Court directed that the presbytery conduct the required investigation and established that credible reports affecting Christian character warrant investigation regardless of the evidentiary standards required for conviction.

artifacts.synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

artifacts.synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.
